items.title: 52263_Sonny Greer oral history interview
items.q: I know one time on a recording session, if Barney Bigard, on clarinet, if he didn't show or was late for the recording, he would give Lawrence Brown a clarinet part.

ctx.x: That's why today those guys are laying in his grave -- they haven't caught us in 25 to 30 years, because it ain't down. Just the basis, and when it comes to a solo and ensembles he wrote those, or have an arranger do it for him, but he knew what he wanted, but like he'd tell Johnny, Tricky, or any of the guys, Lawrence Brown, Tizol, he'd leave it blank. The only thing he'd write, how many choruses he wanted them to play. That's why Johnny Hodges, Carney, there's no more Johnny Hodges, there's no more Harry…

exaggeration, Lawrence Brown was the greatest trombone player I ever heard in my life. Lawrence Brown, you remember Lawrence Brown trying to make -- well, they were always looking for a ofay--- king --/today in prizefighting, but anyway Lawrence Brown, I know one time on a recording session, if Barney Bigard, on clarinet, if he didn't show or was late for the recording, he would give Lawrence Brown a clarinet part. Ever heard of that, a trombone player playing a clarinet part?

And he would run it clean as a whistle. We were in California making a picture and Tommy Dorsey, he said to me, I'll never forget said 'That's the greatest trombone player in the world.' And Lawrence Brown didn't know what he could do, you better believe it. Barney, and a bass player -- Charlie Mingus just died.

items.title: 68113_Barney Bigard oral history interview
items.q: get a few of his men that was in the group, like Sonny, Nance, myself

ctx.x: No, '73, I guess it must have been because he died in '74. It must have been 1973.

Well, -- which was George Wein's idea that he'd like to reminisce, you know, get a few of his men that was in the group, like Sonny, Nance, myself, and somebody else, I don't know. And so George told me, "Get here a little early because Duke is coming in early." He had been working somewhere. I don't know, it was somewhere in Jersey somewhere. And he was coming in for a rehearsal with Nance and Sonny and myself. And so I said, "Okay."

So I came in early and there he was. So he started rehearsing things that he had been playing, I mean, probably all that night. So he said, "What you want to do?" I said, "I'll do something simple." He said, "How about 'Tiger Rag'?" I said, "You must be kidding. 'Tiger Rag'. It's hard. I said simple. Don't you know what simple means?" So he said, "What?" I said, "Rose Room." I said, "Everybody knows 'Rose Room.'" So he said, "Okay." He said, "What tempo?" I said, "You know the right tempo," and I gave him the…
